claims.text: In situ aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy can directly observe atomic-scale structural changes in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles during controlled heating.
Such in situ imaging can test whether thermally driven phase separation, ordering transitions, or defect formation occurs as predicted by thermodynamic models.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The nanoparticles initially form a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution at room temperature.
An ACTEM heating stage can gradually raise the nanoparticle temperature under controlled environmental conditions.
Atomic-resolution imaging can be performed in real time while heating these nanoparticles from room temperature to approximately 700–1000 °C.
Heating in vacuum or inert gas will avoid oxidation of the nanoparticles.
Heating may induce atomic rearrangements, precipitate nucleation, or changes in lattice parameters.
These structural changes can indicate thermodynamic instability or a structural transformation.
Increasing thermal energy enhances atomic mobility in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Enhanced atomic mobility may overcome stabilization attributed to high configurational entropy.
Overcoming configurational-entropy stabilization may cause phase separation or ordering transitions.
Phase separation or ordering transitions can be directly imaged at the atomic scale.
If the thermodynamic predictions are correct, structural changes will begin at identifiable temperature thresholds.
The maximum stable temperature available in TEM and electron-beam-induced damage or artifacts limit the investigation.
Distinguishing thermally induced changes from electron-beam-induced changes may be difficult.
Quantitative attribution of observed changes to particular thermodynamic contributions and determination of exact transition temperatures require calibration against theoretical models.
Selected-area electron diffraction can monitor phase transitions or ordering changes during heating.

A lack of atomic rearrangement, phase separation, or defect evolution beyond beam effects at high temperature would falsify the proposed effect of thermodynamic contributions on structural properties.
